item.title: Rolling-Horizon Distributionally Robust Train Scheduling Model Cuts Delays by Up to 20%
item.description:
Rolling-Horizon Distributionally Robust Train Scheduling Model Cuts Delays by Up to 20%

🔍 Overview

  • Uncertainty in resource reopening times makes train holding and rerouting decisions difficult when closures coincide with arrival delays and longer processing times.
  • A new rolling‑horizon distributionally robust model has been created to address this challenge.

🧩 How it works

  • The model updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as observations of disruption resolution become available.
  • It jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings.
  • The objective is to minimize the worst‑case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities.
  • Solution algorithm GNN‑LBBD:
    • Uses logic‑based Benders decomposition to coordinate routing and resource scheduling.
    • Constructs conditional cuts from resource‑use patterns.
    • Employs a graph neural network to decide the order in which resource‑relaxation subproblems are solved.

⚙️ Key details

  • Tested on 28 instances for a five‑track station.
  • Achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train‑minutes.
  • Compared to benchmarks:
    • 16.63 % lower than tabu search.
    • 20.06 % lower than variable neighborhood search.
    • Mean computation time was close to that of tabu search.
  • Information impact (six representative instances):
    • Using observations of disruption resolution reduced mean delay by ≈21.7 %.
    • Scenario‑based and conditional‑mean predictions gave similar overall results under the same information conditions.
    • Benefits were greater in instances with alternative routes.
  • These findings suggest a link between observation use, station resource structure, and the scope for schedule adjustments.

💡 Why it matters

  • The ability to incorporate real‑time observations into a robust optimization framework enables more reliable train scheduling under uncertain disruptions.
  • The combination of Benders decomposition and graph neural networks provides a scalable approach that outperforms traditional heuristics while keeping computation times practical.
  • Understanding how resource structure influences the value of information can guide future station design and operational policies.

#trainscheduling #robustoptimization #graphneuralnetworks #bendersdecomposition

Source: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions

item.title: Language Models Assist in Detecting Joint Constraint Families for Dantzig‑Wolfe Reformulations
item.description:
Language Models Assist in Detecting Joint Constraint Families for Dantzig‑Wolfe Reformulations

A new study investigates whether large language models can predict which families of constraints need to be added together to strengthen mixed‑integer program relaxations.

🔍 Overview

  • Dantzig‑Wolfe reformulation improves the linear relaxation of a mixed‑integer program by convexifying selected constraint families.
  • The challenge is that some families only strengthen the bound when added jointly, causing naïve sequential searches to stop prematurely.

🧩 How it Works

  • Prediction sources explored:
    • A one‑pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which cannot see groups whose families share no variable.
    • A language model that reads the names and text of the model description.
  • JointDW combines the language‑model prediction with the lookahead, verifying predictions through a staged search while keeping loss bounded.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Joint‑strengthening groups occur in about 25 % of the MIPLIB‑NL models whose bounds can be improved.
  • The strongest language models identify these groups as often as the lookahead does.
  • When predictions rely on model names (textbook models), accuracy matches the lookahead; adding reasoning doubles that accuracy.
  • For larger models with many distracting families:
    • The lookahead finds the group with one evaluation of three families.
    • Language models given only the text rarely name the group.
    • A reasoning‑enabled model that sees every coefficient names the group in all but one answer and needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Identifying constraint groups that only help jointly can reduce the number of costly column‑generation runs.
  • Leveraging language‑model predictions can complement traditional optimization heuristics, potentially accelerating the solution of complex mixed‑integer programs.

Source: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together? Source: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
